sections.h2: Why do Marietta owners open two tax envelopes every fall?
sections.html:
Two governments bill the same house. Cobb County mails a statement for county taxes. The City of Marietta Tax Division mails a second one that rolls up the city levy, Marietta City Schools, the Gateway Marietta Community Improvement District and the Downtown Marietta Development Authority. Paying one leaves the other untouched.

Value is the one thing the two share. Cobb's assessors decide it, and the city applies its own rates to that figure. Real property returns are filed with the Cobb assessors at 736 Whitlock Avenue, Suite 200.

  • Cobb statements go out by August 15 and are due October 15, either received or postmarked by the Postal Service. A metered or kiosk postmark is rejected.
  • City statements for 2026 began mailing August 26, and the city deadline that year was October 31.
  • The city calls a bill delinquent 60 days after mailing and sends it to the owner as of January 1.

The city's tax page describes Marietta's taxes as the lowest of any metro Atlanta city above 10,000 residents. Rates are reset each summer, so quote nobody's old number.

sections.h2: Where can I pay or ask a question in Marietta?
sections.html:
Walk into City Hall at 205 Lawrence Street, first floor, for the city's Tax Division, open from 8 am to 5 pm on weekdays. The phone is 770-794-5680, and a recorded line at 770-794-5130 runs day and night. A drop box at the City Hall parking deck is open at all hours. Online payment sits under How Do I on the city site, and the counter takes cards, checks, cash and money orders.

Cobb runs its main property tax office at 736 Whitlock Avenue and branches on Lower Roswell Road, Canton Road, Austell Road and Kemp Ridge Road. Online, it accepts e-checks, major cards, PayPal, Apple Pay and Google Pay, charging a convenience fee on cards but not on e-checks. The pay-by-phone line is 1-866-535-2622, and mailed checks go to Cobb County Tax Commissioner, P.O. Box 100127, Marietta, GA 30061.

sections.h2: What kind of city is Marietta for a seller?
sections.html:
Marietta predates Atlanta. A plat was drawn in 1833, the legislature recognized the town on December 19, 1834, and the city incorporated in 1852. Like most Georgia towns, it grew around a square with a courthouse. The Western and Atlantic Railroad chose Marietta for its base, tanyards and taverns multiplied, and on April 12, 1862 the raiders of the Great Locomotive Chase boarded their train here. Union troops held the town in 1864 and burned it that November. The Marietta Museum of History sits on the second floor of the Kennesaw House.

The modern city is a dense, mostly renting one by Georgia standards. Census QuickFacts describe it this way.

  • A July 2025 population of 63,574, which is 4.1 percent above the April 2020 base of 61,060.
  • 23.43 square miles of land and 2,602 residents per square mile at the 2020 count.
  • 24,707 households, with owners in 47.2 percent of homes.
  • Owner-occupied homes valued at a median $448,500, rent at $1,586 and owner costs of $2,170 a month with a mortgage.
  • Foreign-born residents at 18.1 percent, adults with a bachelor's degree or higher at 47.4 percent and residents 65 or older at 13.9 percent.
  • Household income of $72,725 at the median and a 27.5 minute average commute.

sections.h2: How do Marietta owners learn their value, and what is the appeal window?
sections.html:
Cobb's assessors mail notices before July 1. Treat the notice as an estimate, not a bill. It reports market value on January 1, shows the old and new values and estimates savings from approved exemptions, though the city warns that city exemptions may be missing from that estimate. The taxed share is 40 percent.

An owner has 45 days to appeal. The city's calendar uses the end of that window as a second deadline for homestead applications. While an appeal is open, Cobb Tax prints two amounts on the bill: the regular tax and a lower appeal amount based on 85 percent of assessed value or 100 percent of the prior value nobody contested. At least the appeal amount is due October 15. The City Tax Division offers an equivalent choice, paying the whole bill or 85 percent of it. If the final value lands after the due date, the owner pays any additional tax with interest.

A buyer files a first return with the Cobb assessors between January 1 and April 1 of the year after purchase. The city stresses that a lawyer does not file it. The assessors need a copy of the warranty deed and the owner's mailing address when it differs from the property address.

sections.h2: Which exemptions does a Marietta homeowner get?
sections.html:
Homestead exemptions apply to a house you own, live in and claim as your legal residence on January 1. The city says to apply by April 1 or within the 45-day appeal window, and only one name on the deed has to sign. Exemptions renew each year unless ownership changes, you stop qualifying or the city asks for a new filing. Apart from the veteran's exemption, the property has to be in the applicant's name, and a postmark on the deadline is enough.

Cobb describes a basic homestead exemption, senior exemptions that begin at age 62 and include a full or reduced school tax exemption, an exemption for 100 percent service-connected disabled veterans, and others for disabled owners, surviving spouses of certain public servants and some nonprofit and religious property.

  • City exemptions are handled by the Marietta Tax Division.
  • County exemptions are handled through Cobb.
  • A business can apply for a freeport inventory exemption with the Cobb assessors from January 1 to April 1, and the city grants a 100 percent exemption on qualifying inventory.

Once you sell, the exemption ends with your ownership. Cobb tells owners who lose eligibility to report it, using the form on the bill or its online request.

sections.h2: What does a late Marietta bill cost?
sections.html:
The city adds monthly interest on delinquent tax at the bank prime loan rate plus 3 percent, expressed as an annual rate that resets in January. A 5 percent penalty follows 120 days past the due date, and again every 120 days, to a maximum of 20 percent. A fi fa, the tax lien, adds its own charges.

Cobb also charges a 5 percent penalty and monthly interest, and says it cannot waive late fees. Its fi fa fee is $23 on taxes under $100 and $33 on taxes over $100, plus administrative costs. An owner who never receives a bill still owes the tax, and Cobb suggests printing the bill online.

Escrow can complicate things. When a mortgage servicer asks for the bill, Cobb sends one to both servicer and owner, and refunds a duplicate payment. The city copies the original to the servicer and a copy to the owner when notified in time. Verify which bill your escrow account actually paid.

sections.h2: How should I clear Marietta taxes before a sale?
sections.html:
In Marietta, taxes follow the property, so the current owner answers for anything outstanding. Call the Tax Division at 770-794-5680 for the city balance and Cobb Tax for the county balance, and ask both for written payoff figures and whether a lien has been filed.

After closing, report the sale and your new mailing address to Cobb in writing. The city says it is your job to contact the Tax Division if an expected bill never shows up.

faqs.q: What are the Marietta property tax due dates?
faqs.a: Cobb County bills are due October 15. City of Marietta bills, mailed from late August, were due October 31 for 2026. Check the date printed on each bill.

faqs.q: Which office bills the City of Marietta tax?
faqs.a: The City of Marietta Tax Division, at 205 Lawrence Street, 770-794-5680. Its bill covers the city, Marietta City Schools, Gateway Marietta CID and the downtown authority.

faqs.q: Who hears a Marietta value appeal?
faqs.a: The Cobb County Board of Tax Assessors receives it, inside 45 days of the notice. The city does not set value and sends valuation questions to the Cobb assessors.

faqs.q: Can I pay less while my appeal is pending?
faqs.a: Yes. The city allows 85 percent of the billed amount by the due date, and Cobb prints a lower appeal amount to be paid by October 15. Interest can apply if the final value arrives later.

faqs.q: Does the buyer or the seller owe the Marietta tax bill?
faqs.a: The tax follows the property, and the current owner is responsible for what is outstanding. Bills go to the January 1 owner, so the sale contract should say who reimburses whom.
